title: Why do we say bless you?

segments.text: Does your heart really stop when you sneeze? That's the old story behind saying bless you.
It doesn't. Your heart keeps beating. A sneeze just changes the pressure in your chest, so one beat can land a little late, and the next one thumps harder. That's the skip you feel.
So where did the blessing come from? A famous story says Pope Gregory ordered it during a plague in {590,|five ninety,} but historians doubt that story.
What we do know: by around {750|seven fifty} AD, saying it was already a custom. Many people believed the soul was a breath of air, and a sneeze could throw it out, or let something evil in.
So bless you was a tiny shield, said in less than a second.
Nobody believes that anymore, but we still say it. Old fears turn into good manners.
So next time someone sneezes, you're not saving their heart. You're keeping a thousand-year-old habit alive. If you enjoyed this, like and follow for more.
